title: Flock Highlighted Police Departments Using Its Tech. Now 4 Face Allegations of Misuse
gist: At least four police departments Flock promoted as showcase customers on its own YouTube channel — Savannah, Albany, Sandy Springs and Baytown — have since faced allegations that officers misused its automatic license plate reader system, with five Albany officers fired and charged by the Georgia Bureau of Investigation. Flock's public defense has shifted from prevention to detection, leaning on an Audit Assistance Program launched in April that flagged 127 inappropriate searches out of 39,000 in Savannah this year.

insights.claim: At least four police departments that automatic license plate reader vendor Flock featured as showcase customers on its YouTube channel — Savannah, Albany, Sandy Springs and Baytown — have subsequently faced allegations that officers misused the company's ALPR technology.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: A vendor's own marketing library is becoming a discovery map for journalists and plaintiffs; surveillance-tech customer testimonials now carry reputational tail risk rather than pure credibility value.
insights.quote: Flock, the increasingly controversial automatic license plate reader (ALPR) company, has previously highlighted at least four police departments on its YouTube page that have since faced allegations of misusing the company’s technology.

insights.claim: Misuse of ALPR systems is not confined to weak or unsophisticated agencies — it has surfaced at departments a vendor selected and publicly promoted as exemplary deployments.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Undercuts the standard vendor argument that misuse is an outlier-agency problem; suggests the failure mode is structural to the product's access model, which is what regulators will target.
insights.quote: While these incidents show that police departments have mechanisms to detect and address ALPR misuse, Flock's promotional materials show that it can occur even at departments that were touted as exemplary.

Persley making explicit privacy assurances to residents — the same department that later fired five officers over ALPR misuse.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Vendor advocacy programs that elevate individual officers into named brand ambassadors concentrate reputational exposure in people the vendor cannot control.

insights.claim: Three of the four implicated showcase departments — Savannah, Albany and Sandy Springs — are in Georgia, where ALPR misuse allegations have also been reported at the sheriff's offices of Coweta, Cherokee, Habersham and Richmond counties.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Georgia is the most likely first mover on state-level ALPR restrictions or audit mandates, which would set the template other states copy and directly shape Flock's addressable market.
insights.quote: In Georgia alone—home to the Savannah, Albany, and Sandy Springs police departments—allegations of ALPR misuse have also been reported at the sheriff’s offices of Coweta County, Cherokee County, Habersham County, and Richmond County.

insights.claim: ALPR misuse allegations have spread beyond Georgia to police departments in Kansas, North Carolina, Ohio and Wisconsin, making it a multi-state pattern rather than a regional anomaly.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Geographic breadth raises the odds of federal or multi-state legislative attention, a step-change in regulatory risk versus scattered local incidents.
insights.locator: Allegations of ALPR misuse have plagued police departments across the country

insights.claim: The Georgia Bureau of Investigation charged five fired Albany officers with misuse of license plate data and violating their oaths of office, escalating ALPR misuse from an HR matter into criminal exposure.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Criminal charges create a precedent and a discovery record; each prosecution generates documentation of how the system was queried, which is the raw material for future litigation and legislation.
insights.quote: The Georgia Bureau of Investigation charged the officers for misuse of license plate data and violating their oaths of office.

insights.claim: Enforcement actions against the featured departments clustered tightly in a matter of weeks: Albany fired five officers on July 6, Baytown's chief announced an officer's resignation on July 30, and Savannah's mayor referred six employees to the GBI on July 31.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Simultaneous timing suggests either a common triggering audit capability or contagion of scrutiny — either way, expect more disclosures in the following weeks rather than a contained episode.

themes.theme: Audit tooling as the vendor's defense

insights.claim: Flock's public position is that detected misuse validates rather than indicts the product, with spokesperson Paris Lewbel arguing that investigations and firings are 'evidence that oversight mechanisms are working.'
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: This reframing — abuse detected equals system working — is the reusable defense every surveillance vendor will deploy; watch whether regulators accept it, because if they don't, audit features stop being a shield.
insights.quote: When improper use is detected, agencies can investigate, take action, and hold individuals accountable. That should be viewed as evidence that oversight mechanisms are working
insights.locator: In response to WIRED’s request for comment

insights.claim: Flock introduced a Flock Safety Audit Assistance Program in April that 'continuously monitors system activity and surfaces search patterns that fall outside an agency's typical usage,' and Savannah's internal investigation ran through that program.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: The vendor is monetizing and productizing the remedy for its own risk; compliance/audit tooling is becoming a required attach-on for surveillance sales rather than an optional feature.
insights.quote: continuously monitors system activity and surfaces search patterns that fall outside an agency’s typical usage
insights.locator: According to Johnson, the Savannah Police Department conducted an internal investigation

insights.claim: Savannah police chief Lenny Gunther said the audit surfaced 127 inappropriate searches out of 39,000 conducted this year — roughly a 0.3 percent misuse rate at a single department.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: The first concrete base rate for ALPR query misuse; applied across a national deployment footprint it implies a very large absolute number of improper searches, which is the number critics will extrapolate.
insights.quote: the investigation surfaced 127 inappropriate searches out of the 39,000 it conducted this year
insights.locator: Savannah police chief Lenny Gunther told a local news outlet

insights.claim: That an audit tool launched in April is what surfaced the Savannah violations implies the misuse was occurring undetected beforehand, meaning the detection rate reflects tooling coverage rather than the true incidence of abuse.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Expect a wave of newly discovered historical misuse as more agencies enable audit monitoring — a rising disclosure curve that looks like deterioration but is really improved measurement.

insights.claim: A Sandy Springs officer was terminated after allegedly running ALPR searches to support beta testing for Signal 8, a law enforcement software company that employed him in a second job, and refusing to cooperate with the internal investigation.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Shows a commercial leakage channel — officers with side employment at adjacent vendors using police surveillance data as free product-development input; a compliance vector nobody is currently auditing for.
insights.quote: the officer allegedly ran ALPR searches to support beta testing for Signal 8, a law enforcement software company that employed the officer in a second job

insights.claim: Baytown's chief John Stringer disclosed that the officer accused of misusing Flock faced two parallel investigations, one internal and one criminal, and resigned on July 30 while both remained ongoing.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Resignation ahead of resolution is the pattern that frustrates accountability advocates and fuels demands for statutory penalties rather than employment-based remedies.
insights.quote: Accountability to the fullest extent of the law will be pursued

insights.claim: Savannah's response involved four officers and two civilian workers placed on administrative leave over 'potential misuses,' indicating ALPR access extends beyond sworn officers to non-sworn department staff.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Broader internal access surface than commonly assumed; any policy fix limited to sworn officers would miss a third of the implicated users in this case.
insights.quote: Four officers and two workers from the department were recently placed on administrative leave after an internal investigation found “potential misuses” of Flock’s ALPR system.
insights.locator: The company featured the Savannah Police Department in a March 2022 YouTube video

insights.claim: A Baytown officer described Flock in the company's own 2025 promotional video as the first application he opens after logging in and something used 'multiple times every day,' evidencing deep daily workflow embedding.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: High daily-usage stickiness makes departmental churn unlikely even amid scandal — the commercial risk to Flock is legislative and contractual, not voluntary customer attrition.
insights.quote: We use it multiple times every day, and once I log in to my computer, Flock is the first thing I click on

insights.claim: Flock's marketing has consistently sold the technology through low-stakes, sympathetic use cases — porch pirates in the 2020 Sandy Springs video, a carjacking in the 2025 Baytown video, property crime and 'crimes of opportunity' in Albany — rather than through its broader surveillance capability.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: The gap between the narrow marketed use case and the actual query capability is exactly where misuse occurs and where legislators will draw purpose-limitation lines.
insights.locator: Flock also highlighted the Sandy Springs Police Department in a 2020 video

insights.claim: Public officials are converging on a 'public trust is non-negotiable' framing — Savannah mayor Van Johnson's phrasing — that separates the tool's legitimacy from individual misuse, giving vendors political cover to keep contracts intact.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: As long as officials blame users rather than the system, contract cancellations stay rare; the signal to watch is the first municipality that terminates rather than audits.
insights.quote: These tools exist to keep our community safe, not for personal or unauthorized use.

insights.claim: None of the three implicated departments contacted — Albany, Savannah and Baytown — responded to press requests for comment, leaving the vendor as the sole voice defending the deployments.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Customer silence pushes the entire narrative burden onto Flock, concentrating headline risk on the company rather than diffusing it across agencies.
insights.locator: The Albany Police Department did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment
